newsitem.title: CHINA: HK govt faces mounting pressure in courtroom.
newsitem.headline: HK govt faces mounting pressure in courtroom.

text.p: Hong Kong's political fate hung in the balance on Thursday as a court case adjourned pending a judgment next week that could plunge the post-colonial government into a constitutional crisis.
The landmark court challenge centres on the China-appointed Provisional Legislative Council, which top lawyers have argued violates Hong Kong's new constitution.
Wrapping up the appeal court hearing, a top government lawyer said that any bid by the court to declare the interim chamber illegal would invite chaos and jeopardise the entire legal system.
Presiding Chief Judge Justice Patrick Chan said his panel would make a judgment next Tuesday.
Legal experts said it was up to Chan's team whether to rule on the legality of the legislature, a case that grew from a criminal conspiracy trial into a constitutional conundrum.

Lawyers argued that three defendants charged with criminal conspiracy should be set free because the pre-handover laws under which they were charged ceased to be valid on July 1 when the chamber failed formally to adopt them, leaving a legal vacuum.
The argument throws into doubt the status and legality of the Provisional Legislature, installed to replace an elected chamber when Britain handed its 156-year-old colony back to China on July 1.
The challenge is at the heart of the legal system and Hong Kong institutions, as the chamber has endorsed the appointment of senior judges and passed crucial laws since it was sworn in 24 days ago.

In a packed court room, Solicitor-General Daniel Fung argued that the provisional chamber, cobbled together by a China-appointed body and endorsed by China's parliament in April, was a legal necessity with the end of British rule and the entry of the new sovereign power, China.

Fung said China axed original plans to allow the 1995 chamber to serve its full four-year term beyond the handover because 1995 electoral rules spearheaded by the last colonial governor Chris Patten did not conform to a Sino-British treaty.
He said it was not up to Hong Kong courts to rule on decisions of China's parliament, and any attempt to declare the chamber null and void would lead to havoc.
"If your lordships were to rule against us ... there would be no legal system. The rule of law exists to protect people, and cannot be used to destroy society," he said.

But former Bar chairwoman Gladys Li said judges had the right to rule on the legality of the chamber, which she argued had no basis in Hong Kong's new constitution and violated 1990 rules for the first post-handover assembly set by China's parliament.

Meanwhile, the post-colonial government hit out at critics over its decision to roll back a set of labour rights laws, saying they had been passed with "indecent haste" in the last days of British rule and needed careful review.
"From the government's point of view, we asked for these bills to be suspended to give us time to look at them," commissioner for labour Jacqueline Willis told reporters.
"Does this mean that we're turning back the clock? I can assure you we are not doing that."
Last week, the unelected Provisional Legislature endorsed a bill freezing until October laws on collective bargaining, use of trade union funds and anti-union discrimination by employers.

The move, ostensibly on the grounds that the three laws may hurt Hong Kong's competitiveness, sparked an uproar among local pro-democracy unions and labour groups world wide, who bombarded the territory's leader Tung Chee-hwa with letters of protest.

Hong Kong University's latest opinion poll found nearly 44 percent of people polled were less confident in the territory's rule of law after the government froze the labour laws. Only 1.7 percent were more confident.
